claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a single-phase high-temperature BCC state.
Phase stability in this alloy is governed by the interplay between thermodynamically driven compositional ordering and kinetically limited diffusion during post-processing annealing.
Annealing temperature alters diffusional recovery processes, particularly those involving Al.
Annealing-induced diffusion modifies local chemical order.
The resulting local chemical order predisposes the quenched alloy either to retain BCC or to form a secondary phase state.
Short-range diffusion of Al and other elements mediates transformation from metastable high-temperature BCC to retained BCC or a mixed-phase state.
Above a critical annealing-temperature threshold, increased atomic mobility enables rapid diffusive homogenization.
Rapid diffusive homogenization at temperatures above the threshold maintains or re-establishes the high-temperature BCC arrangement.
Water quenching freezes in the BCC arrangement established above the threshold.
Below the threshold, kinetically limited diffusion produces incipient elemental partitioning and local compositional fluctuations.
Incipient partitioning and local compositional fluctuations favor nucleation of a secondary phase.
Samples annealed above the threshold will largely retain high-temperature BCC after water quenching.
Samples annealed just below the threshold will develop secondary phases or mixed-phase microstructures.
The below-threshold phase transformation will be accompanied by detectable local compositional changes.
The controlled comparison holds annealing time and quenching rate constant while varying annealing temperature.
The unannealed high-temperature single-phase BCC alloy is the experimental control.
The hypothesis is restricted to rapid water quenching after controlled annealing and may not apply under slow cooling.
The hypothesis may not transfer to substantially different compositions because their diffusion kinetics and thermodynamic driving forces differ.
The critical annealing temperature and relevant diffusion rates are not yet quantified.
Absence of a systematic relationship between annealing temperature and secondary-phase emergence or suppression would falsify the proposed mechanism.
